info.title: Lenz — AI Fact-Checking API
info.description:
# Four API calls and one to run them

A research-depth ladder: find claims, judge fast, prove deep, citecheck; `/review` runs them all.

- `POST /extract` — enumerate every major verifiable claim in a document (up to 100, most check-worthy first, inputs to 50k chars), or in a public web page given its URL; an optional `focus` narrows the list to the claims you care about, and `locate: true` keeps only the claims traced back to the text, with where each is made. Costs no credits; fair-use cap 1,000/account/day.
- `POST /assess` — fast 3-model frontier panel verdict, typically 10-25s. Sync, 1 credit per claim. Send one text in `claim`, or a list of up to 20 in `claims` — one row per claim, same order, all checked in parallel. A text that makes more claims than one call checks gets the most check-worthy checked and the rest back as `more_claims`, free, to send on.
- `POST /verify` — full multi-model pipeline with citations in ~90s. Async, 10 credits — or 5 with `depth: "low"`, a shallower check that comes back sooner.
- `POST /citecheck` — does each cited source say what the text attributes to it: send pairs of a statement and its URL or DOI, or a whole text. Async; 1 credit per checked citation, refunded when a citation could not be checked ([guide](https://lenz.io/docs/citations)).
- `POST /review` — the extract → assess → verify ladder on a whole draft, returning the issues with suggested rewrites in 2-4 min. Async, 1 credit per claim assessed + 10 (5 at `depth: "low"`) per claim verified. With `escalate.max_citations` (0-20, default 0) it also checks whether each source the draft cites says what the draft attributes to it, at 1 credit per checked citation (one that could not be checked is refunded) ([guide](https://lenz.io/docs/citations)). `more_claims` and `more_citations` list what the review found and did not check, at no cost; send them to `/assess` and `/citecheck` to check the rest.
- Also `POST /ask/{id}` — ask follow-up questions grounded on a verification.

## Built for teams whose AI output is async or document-shaped

Legal-memo generators, AI deep-research, due-diligence platforms, vertical agents producing structured deliverables, "report-as-a-service" companies. `/assess` opens the door to sync UX too — fast enough to gate a chat completion or a UI submit.

## Install the SDK

```bash
pip install lenz-io      # Python
npm install lenz-io      # Node / TypeScript
```

Source on GitHub: [lenz-io-python](https://github.com/lenzhq/lenz-io-python) · [lenz-io-node](https://github.com/lenzhq/lenz-io-node).

## The canonical integration: one /review call

```python
from lenz_io import Lenz
client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")

# Extract, assess, and verify the doubtful claims in one call (async, 2-4 min)
draft = "The EU AI Act took effect in March 2024. It sorts AI systems into four risk tiers."
review = client.review_and_wait(text=draft)
for i in review.issues:
    print(i.verdict, i.claim, i.suggested_rewrite)
```

The default policy: a quick verdict on every claim (up to 20), and the deep check on the rows whose quick verdict is `False`, `Mostly False` or `Mixed`, or whose confidence is `low`, up to five. Change it in `escalate`. To deep-check the rows the cap left out (`escalation.disposition == "cap"`), send them to `/verify/batch`. A resend with the same `Idempotency-Key` within 24 hours returns the same review; a new key is a new review.

## The primitives, call by call: extract → assess → conditional verify

```python
from lenz_io import Lenz
client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")

# 1. Enumerate the factual claims in your model output (free)
# identified_claims is the complete ordered list when >1 claim is
# found (top claim included — iterate it alone); for a single claim
# it is [] and the claim lives in .claim.
# Pass focus="market size and competitors" to narrow the list;
# status is "no_match" when the document has claims but none match.
extracted = client.extract(text=llm_output)
claims = extracted.identified_claims or [extracted.claim]

# 2. Fast verdict on every claim in ONE call (typically 10-25s, 3-model panel):
# a list of up to 20, one row per claim, in the order you sent them.
quick = client.assess(claims=claims).claims

# 3. Escalate the low-confidence ones to /verify in one batch (~90s, multi-model pipeline)
# Rows we ran out of time on are free and worth resending; the rest of the
# Error rows (no_claim, framing_failed) want a different input.
retry = [c.claim for c in quick if c.error_code == "timeout"]
quick += client.assess(claims=retry).claims if retry else []
doubtful = [{"claim": c.claim} for c in quick if c.verdict != "Error" and c.confidence == "low"]
for r in client.verify_batch_and_wait(claims=doubtful) if doubtful else []:
    if r.verification:
        print(r.verification.verdict, r.verification.lenz_score, r.verification.key_finding)
```

## How /verify works under the hood

Frame → Collect Evidence → Debate (2 models, 2 rounds) → Adjudicate (three reviewers on models from different vendors, two more when they disagree) → Conclude. ~90 seconds wall-clock per claim.

### While /verify is running

`GET /verify/status/{task_id}` answers one of four shapes, keyed on `status`: `processing`, `needs_input`, `completed`, `failed`. Every one echoes `task_id`, and only the fields belonging to that shape are present — read the ones for the branch you are in, and treat an absent key as absent rather than empty.

A `processing` body carries `progress`:

```json
{"status": "processing", "task_id": "…",
 "progress": {"step": "research", "index": 2, "total": 5,
              "elapsed_seconds": 42, "poll_after_seconds": 5}}
```

`step` is a closed set — `starting`, `framing`, `research`, `debate`, `adjudication`, `conclusion` — so it is safe to switch on. `index` is the 1-based stage position (0 while `starting`) out of `total`; read `total` off the response rather than hard-coding it. `poll_after_seconds` is how long to wait before looking again, and `elapsed_seconds` is how long the run has been going — a measurement, not an estimate of what is left.

Note that `index` is stage **position**, not elapsed work: the stages are uneven, so a progress bar driven by it will sit on `research` for roughly half the run.

`progress` is **advisory**. It says the work is pending and which stage it is on; it is not a place to read results from. The verdict arrives once, under `result`, when `status` is `completed`.

### When /verify asks for input

`/verify` is not only submit-and-poll. `GET /verify/status/{task_id}` can terminate at `needs_input` — the submitted text held several claims, or was too vague to check as written — and the task waits rather than guessing which claim you meant. Several claims in one sentence count the same as several sentences.

Resolve it with `POST /verify/{task_id}/select`, passing the exact wording of the claim(s) you want from the ones the status offered. Selection is **by text, not index**; anything that was not offered is rejected with a 422. Each selected claim fans out into its own pipeline, so the response carries one `task_id` per claim — poll each the way you would a fresh `/verify`.

Claims returned by `/extract` skip this entirely: submitted verbatim, they are never bounced back for rephrasing.

### Covered verification

Every verification a paid Pro or Scale account runs is put in front of a gate. The ones that qualify carry a contractual warranty, and every result tells you whether it qualified — a `coverage` block on the completed `/verify/status/{task_id}` body, on `GET /verifications/{id}` and on the `verification.completed` webhook.

It is on by default, with no request field to set; an account on Pro or Scale can turn certificates off on the API credentials page, for checks submitted from then on (reason `account`; a verification that already carries a certificate keeps it).

`status` is `covered`, `pending_timestamp` or `uncovered`; `reasons` says why not, in a closed seven-value vocabulary. **If you publish automatically, key on the `certificate.timestamped` webhook, not `verification.completed`** — cover requires the qualified timestamp to precede what you publish, and `completed` fires while the qualified timestamp is still pending.

Full wire format, the reason vocabulary and the offline verifier: [lenz.io/docs/coverage](https://lenz.io/docs/coverage). What is covered and what is not: [lenz.io/warranty](https://lenz.io/warranty).

### When /verify fails

A `failed` status (and the `verification.failed` webhook) carries two axes. `failure_reason` says **where** the pipeline stopped (`research_empty`, `conclusion_failed`, `task_stuck`, …); on the webhook the same value rides in `error`. `failure_class` says **why**, and `retryable` is derived from it:

| `failure_class` | Meaning | `retryable` |
|---|---|---|
| `upstream_unavailable` | Model or search providers were rate-limited or down, or the task was never run — resubmit after a short wait | `true` |
| `insufficient_evidence` | We looked; the sources are not there | `false` |
| `invalid_input` | Not a checkable claim, an unreadable URL | `false` |
| `cancelled` | You stopped it | `false` |
| `internal` | Anything else — retrying the same input will not help | `false` |

Branch on `retryable`, not on `failure_reason`: the same reason can mean either. `failure_class` is a **closed set** — these five values are stable identifiers. `failure_reason` is an open, informational set (`task_error`, `task_stuck`, `not_a_claim`, … will appear). A failed body also carries `docs_url`, pointing at the explanation of its class. A failed `/verify` is not charged.

One of those reasons comes from framing rather than from a pipeline step and carries `failure_class: invalid_input`: `not_a_claim` (the input is not a checkable statement, or is too vague to have a checkable reading). A vague input that has a likely reading is verified on it, and the result's `claim` is that reading. On the webhook the same value rides in `error`, as an ordinary `verification.failed` delivery; before 2026-09-03 it fired nothing at all, so a task submitted with a `webhook_url` could terminate in silence.

### What may change without notice

New keys may be added to status and webhook bodies at any time — ignore keys you do not recognise. Fields documented as **advisory** — `progress` and everything inside it — may also change or disappear without a version bump. The verdict fields under `result` may not: those change only with a versioned, announced release.

## Common patterns

- **Runtime sync UX**: `POST /assess` on the user-facing path; escalate `confidence == "low"` claims to `/verify` in the background.
- **Runtime webhook**: `POST /verify` with `webhook_url`. Lenz POSTs the typed payload when done. Best for document pipelines.
- **Whole drafts**: `POST /review` with `webhook_url`; handle `review.completed` (a `ReviewWebhookPayload`, deduped on `event_id`) and read `review.issues[]` and `review.citation_issues[]`.
- **CI / pre-release**: `/extract` + batch `/verify` your golden set on every deploy. The free `/extract` tier covers most of this. Claims returned by `/extract` verify cleanly — submitted verbatim to `/verify`, they are never bounced back for rephrasing.
- **Incident triage**: paste the offending output into `/extract`, then `/verify` the wrong-looking claims. Get a citation trail to send back to the customer.

## What's in the response

Unified vocabulary across every claim-shaped response:

- **`claim`** — the framed claim text.
- **`verdict`** — `"True" | "Mostly True" | "Mixed" | "Mostly False" | "False" | "Error"`.
- **`confidence`** — `"high" | "medium" | "low"`.
- **`lenz_score`** — 1–10 integer score (deep payloads).
- **`key_finding`** — one declarative sentence stating the most important fact the analysis established. For a false claim it states the CORRECTED fact rather than restating the claim, so render it next to the verdict label, never as a standalone headline. `""` on older verifications predating the field.
- **`suggested_rewrite`** — a suggested rewrite of `claim` that the verification's findings support. It has not been verified itself: before using it, review it or run it through `/verify`. `null` for a true claim, when no correction is established, and on older verifications. On every verification, single or listed (`GET /verifications/{id}`, `/verify/status`, the `verification.completed` webhook, `GET /verifications`, `GET /library`). On `/assess` rows too when the request sets `suggest_rewrite`: written from the quick check's reasoning for a claim it found False or Mostly False with high confidence, at no extra credit; `null` otherwise, and on every row when not requested.
- **`sources`** — evidence with title, URL and snippet: the sentence(s) quoted from the page, verbatim and in the page's own language (`/verify` only).
- **`audit`** — adjudication reasoning, debate transcript, panel agreement (`/verify` only).

## How the API is organized

- **Extract** — pull verifiable claims out of text.
- **Assess** — fast 3-model verdict.
- **Verify** — deep multi-model pipeline: submit one claim or a batch, poll status, and resolve a `needs_input` interrupt by selecting claims.
- **Verifications** — list, fetch, delete, and toggle visibility on stored verifications.
- **Library** — browse the public catalog. No API key needed.
- **Ask** — follow-up questions, 1 credit each.
- **Account** — your credit balance and the price list.

## Credits

One pool per account funds every billable call, at a fixed weight:

| Endpoint | Credits |
|---|---|
| `POST /verify` (and `/verify/batch`, `/select`) | 10 per claim |
| `POST /verify` with `depth: "low"` | 5 per claim |
| `POST /assess` | 1 per claim — per row that carries a verdict; error rows and rows answered from the cache are free |
| `POST /ask` | 1 |
| `POST /extract` | 0 — free, fair-use capped |

`depth: "low"` caps research breadth — fewer discovery queries, a hard extraction ceiling, no recovery tiers on the happy path — while every reasoning step runs unchanged. It is not a model downgrade. You are charged for the depth you REQUESTED. A `/verify/batch` may mix depths per item and is billed per item.

An answer served from the last hour's cache is free: a `/verify`, `/assess` or `/review` claim that gets back a verdict checked in the last hour costs nothing, so a tool that resends a request is not charged twice. The exception is a `/verify` that issues you a new warranty certificate, charged at the depth you requested.

`GET /me/usage` reports the balance under `credits` and the weights under `costs`, with parameter-dependent prices such as `depth` nested under `cost_options`. The per-capability blocks beside them (`verify`, `assess`, `ask`) are **projections** of that one balance into each capability's own unit — how many of those calls the remaining credits would buy — not separate allowances. Spending on any one of them moves all of them.

## Authentication

1. [Create a Lenz account](https://lenz.io/auth).
2. Generate an API key on the [API credentials](https://lenz.io/api-credentials) page.
3. Send it on every request:
   ```
   Authorization: Bearer lenz_...
   ```

Or skip steps 1–2: **[lenz.io/setup](https://lenz.io/setup)** issues a test key and generates setup instructions for your environment — MCP client, SDK or plain HTTP — that you paste into your coding agent to do the wiring.

### One balance, whichever door you come through

Lenz also runs a remote MCP server at `https://lenz.io/mcp`, so an agent can fact-check inside a conversation. It is **not** part of this surface — there are no MCP endpoints below, and its tools are documented at [lenz.io/integrations/mcp-server](https://lenz.io/integrations/mcp-server).

It matters here for one reason: that server is a client of this API. It takes the same `lenz_...` key and forwards it to the endpoints below, so MCP traffic spends the same credits, counts against the same rate limits, and shows up in `GET /me/usage` — there is no separate MCP quota to check, and a 402 can just as easily be an agent as your own code.

## Idempotency

Send an `Idempotency-Key` header on `POST /extract`, `POST /assess`, `POST /verify`, `POST /verify/batch` and `POST /ask/{verification_id}` so retries after a network drop do not spawn duplicate tasks or double-debit quota. The server caches the response body and returns it on replay; a re-used key with a different body returns 422. The SDKs auto-generate a key for `verify_and_wait`; on other calls pass `idempotency_key` yourself.

On `/ask` a key also keeps the retry out of the conversation: without one, a repeated question is a second turn, a second credit and a second answer that the next turn reads as context. A retry that lands while the first call is still running gets 409 rather than the reply — nothing is finalized yet to replay — so treat it as work already in progress and retry the same key once the first call has had time to finish. `GET /ask/{verification_id}` returns the message history, but carries no request id, so it can only tell you which answer was yours when one question is in flight at a time. The SDKs send the header when you pass a key yourself: `ask.send(..., idempotency_key=...)` in Python, `ask.send(id, { message, idempotencyKey })` in Node; neither generates one for ask, because a repeated question is usually deliberate. The n8n node's Ask operation sends a key scoped to the workflow execution, so a retry replays rather than re-asks. The Zapier app sends none on ask.

## Errors

The status code says what to do next; the body says what happened. Every response carries an `X-Request-ID` header — quote it on a support ticket.

| Status | Condition | Retry? |
|---|---|---|
| 401 | Missing, malformed or unknown key | After fixing credentials |
| 402 | Out of credits, or the plan is the limit | No — billing action |
| 403 | Authenticated but not allowed (private verification, IP block) | No |
| 409 | An identical request is already in flight | Yes, shortly |
| 422 | Malformed input | No |
| 429 | Rate limit (the per-account `/extract` daily cap) | Yes, after `Retry-After` |
| 502 | A sync step (`/assess`, `/extract`) failed deterministically — a schema or parse failure | No — same input, same outcome |
| 503 | Our model providers were rate-limited or down for the step and every fallback was exhausted (`code: upstream_unavailable`), or the pipeline has no capacity (`code: capacity`) | Yes, after `Retry-After` (body `retry_after` too) |

**402** carries `detail`, `code` (always `no_credits`), `upgrade_url`, `doc_url`, `wall_id`, `cost` (what the rejected call would have taken), and — when resolvable — `remaining`, `credits_remaining` and `resets_at`. `remaining` and `requested` are in the *capability's* unit (verifications, assesses); `credits_remaining` and `cost` are in credits, so a client can tell "not enough for a 10-credit verify" from "empty". The resolvable fields are omitted rather than sent as `null`, so an absent key means "unknown", not "zero".

`wall_id` identifies this specific rejection and is already appended to `upgrade_url`, so sending a user to that URL is all that is needed — it exists as its own field only for clients that build their own upgrade link. Treat `upgrade_url` as opaque and follow it whole rather than matching it against a fixed string.

The `code` values are deliberately plan-agnostic: they name the condition, never the plan that would fix it. Send users to `upgrade_url` rather than mapping codes to plan names — the set of plans changes, the conditions do not.

An empty balance is deliberately **not** a 429: a 429 tells every client to retry, and an empty balance never succeeds on retry. **429** carries `code`, `limit`, `reset_in_seconds`, `upgrade_url` and the `Retry-After` header.

**Migrating (August 2026).** These rejections were 403, which the SDKs map to their auth error; they are now 402, which maps to the quota error — not a subclass. If you catch the auth error to handle an empty balance, that branch stops firing. This reaches you on every SDK version, including ones released before the change. `detail` strings are unchanged. Full reference: [lenz.io/docs/errors](https://lenz.io/docs/errors#quota).

## Webhooks

On `POST /verify` and `POST /review` you may supply a `webhook_url`. We POST an HMAC-SHA256-signed JSON payload to it when the pipeline terminates. Signature header is `X-Lenz-Signature: sha256=<hex>`. Verify with your webhook secret (generate + rotate on [API credentials](https://lenz.io/api-credentials)). Retries: 10s, 60s, 600s (3 retries after the initial delivery, 4 attempts total). The SDKs ship a `LenzWebhooks` helper that verifies signatures and parses the payload into typed events. Events: `verification.completed`, `verification.failed`, `certificate.timestamped`, and for a review `review.completed` / `review.failed` (switch on `event`; a review's own deep checks fire no `verification.*` events).

For commercial use, volume pricing, or onboarding support, [get in touch](https://lenz.io/contact).

get.description:
Service discovery root — links to docs, OpenAPI spec, and endpoints.

Returned at ``GET /api/v1/`` so curious humans and probing clients
get a useful JSON payload instead of a 404.

Search and browse the public catalog of verified claims.

Returns paginated results from the Lenz Library. Only publicly
published verifications are included.

**Sort options:** `recent`, `most_true`, `most_untrue`,
`relevance` (only when `search` is provided), and `random`.

**`curated`** restricts results to one or more named curated collections,
comma-separated. Currently supported: `trivia` (the LLM-curated,
trivia-worthy pool behind the open-source quiz demo).

**`verdict`** filters to one or more verdict labels, comma-separated
(e.g. `True,False`). Labels: `True`, `Mostly True`, `Mixed`,
`Mostly False`, `False`.

from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz()  # no api_key needed for the public library
page = client.library.list(page=1, sort="recent")
for v in page.items:
    print(v.claim, "→", v.verdict)

post.description:
Submit a claim for verification.

The claim goes in ``claim``. (``text`` is accepted as an alias — a
document is ``text``, a claim is ``claim``; ``POST /extract`` is the
endpoint that takes a document.)

Returns a ``task_id`` immediately. Poll ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}``
or supply ``webhook_url`` in the body for an asynchronous callback when
the pipeline terminates.

**Duplicate submissions are collapsed.** With no ``Idempotency-Key``
header, the request body itself is the key: resubmitting an identical
body within 10 minutes returns the original ``task_id`` instead of
starting a second run. To run the same text twice on purpose, send your
own ``Idempotency-Key`` — a supplied key always wins.

**``depth``** selects how much work the check does. ``standard``
(default) is the full pipeline. ``low`` searches fewer sources, skips
the recovery fetch tiers and stops the debate after the opening
arguments (no rebuttal round), so it comes back sooner — with less
evidence behind the verdict. Framing, the adjudication panel and the
conclusion run unchanged, and every step runs the same models either
way; ``low`` is a volume lever, not a model downgrade.

``low`` costs **half the credits**, and you are charged for the depth you
REQUESTED. A claim answered from a check made in the last hour is free
(unless it issues you a new warranty certificate, which is charged at the
depth you requested). The completed result echoes the depth the verdict
was actually produced with, which is why that field can read ``standard``
on a ``low`` request: the echo describes the evidence.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
v = client.verify_and_wait(claim="Sharks don't get cancer")
# Add language="es" for Spanish output (12 languages supported).
# Add depth="low" for a shallower check that returns sooner.
print(v.verdict, v.lenz_score)
# false 2.0

post.description:
Fan-out wrapper around /verify for multi-claim LLM responses.

Body: ``{claims: [{text, source_url?, webhook_url?, visibility?, depth?},
...]}`` capped at 20 items. Server pre-checks total credits, then fans out N
independent pipelines — each with its own ``task_id`` and lifecycle.
Each claim's webhook (per-item override, or batch ``webhook_url``, or
per-key default) fires when its pipeline terminates. ``batch_id`` is
purely for client-side correlation; the server doesn't gate anything
on it.

On a mid-fan-out enqueue error, the response includes the partial
``items`` list and a ``partial: true`` flag. Per-claim credit spend
happens at each claim's normal persist time — claims that never
enqueue are never charged.

``depth`` works like ``visibility``: a batch-wide default that any item
can override. See ``POST /verify`` for what the values mean.

Each item carries its claim in ``claim`` (``text`` is accepted as an
alias), plus the same optional fields as ``POST /verify``.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
batch = client.verify_batch(claims=[
    {"text": "The Eiffel Tower is in Berlin."},
    {"text": "Water boils at 100°C at sea level."},
])
for item in batch.items:
    print(item.task_id, item.claim_text)

post.description:
Fast verdict via a 3-model panel (sync, ~10-25s).

Escalation contract: a ``claims[].claim`` text POSTed back verbatim to
``/verify`` within 24 hours is verified as-is — in normal operation it
does not return ``needs_input`` and its wording is not rewritten.

Two input forms, one response shape::

    claim / text  ─► ONE text. Lenz reads the claims in it, and each becomes a
                     row, up to 20 a call; the rest go back, unchecked and
                     free, in ``more_claims``.
    claims[]      ─► a LIST of up to 20 items, each one claim. One row per item, same order.
                     A compound item is assessed on its primary reading and
                     the rest is listed in that row's ``identified_claims``.

The list form is the batch rung of the extract → assess → verify ladder:
one ``/assess`` call answers up to 20 of ``/extract``'s claims (it finds up
to 100) in about the time a single call takes, because every item is
assessed in parallel.

A verdict can be served from memory: a completed ``/verify`` of the exact
same claim text, or a prior ``/assess`` of it, within the last hour,
whichever account ran it — the verdict is a function of the input.
``verification_url`` is set only when the caller could read that
verification by id.

Billing: 1 credit per row that carries a verdict; error rows are free; a
duplicate item is a second row and a second credit (the panel runs once).

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
out = client.assess(text="Coffee causes cancer and the earth is flat.")
# Add language="es" for Spanish verdict text; verdict labels stay English.
for c in out.claims:
    print(c.claim, "→", c.verdict, c.confidence)
    if c.rationale:
        print("  ", c.rationale)

# Several claims at once: one row per item, same order (up to 20).
rows = client.assess(claims=["Coffee causes cancer.", "The earth is flat."]).claims
for c in rows:
    print(c.verdict if c.error_code is None else c.hint)
    if c.dissent:
        print("   One reviewer disagreed:", c.dissent)

post.description:
Extract verifiable claims from arbitrary text.

Runs the extraction step on its own — no research, no debate, no credit
charge. Enumerates every distinct major factual
claim in the input (up to 100), ordered most-check-worthy-first.
`identified_claims` is the complete ordered list when more than one
claim is found — iterate it alone; don't concatenate it with `claim`
(the top claim appears in both). Claims returned here verify cleanly
when submitted verbatim to `POST /verify`.

Pass `focus` to narrow the result to the claims you care about — a short
description such as `"market size, growth and competitors"`, at most 300
characters. A focus selects from the claims the extractor found and
nothing else: it cannot add a claim, reword one, reorder them, change the
language, or change what counts as a claim. Ordering stays
most-check-worthy-first.

`status` is one of:

- `ready` — claims were found (and, with a `focus`, at least one matched).
- `not_a_claim` — the input contains no verifiable factual claim at all.
- `no_match` — claims were found but none fall within your `focus`. The
  unfocused list is never substituted; widen the focus and call again.

`text` can also be a single public web page URL (http or https, nothing
else in the field). Lenz reads the page, or a YouTube video's transcript,
and extracts the claims from its first 50,000 characters. Pages behind a
login (Facebook, Instagram, Threads, LinkedIn) can't be read. A URL call
typically takes 5-40 seconds, so give it a 90-second client timeout (SDK
2.13 and later do). A page that cannot be read answers 502
`extraction_failed`; when the services that read pages are down, 503
`upstream_unavailable` with `Retry-After`. Neither uses a unit of the
daily cap.

Pass `locate: true` to keep only the claims that can be traced directly
back to your text, and get `locations`: for each returned claim, the
passages that make it, with `start` / `end` offsets into `text` as you
sent it, in Unicode code points. A claim the text does not make, or makes
with a different figure, is left out, so the list says what the author
wrote and nothing else. Offsets count code points, not UTF-16 units: in
JavaScript slice with `Array.from(text).slice(start, end).join('')`.
For a URL the offsets are `null` and each position carries its passage.
Locating adds a few seconds, never more than 20. If it cannot run,
`locations` is `null` and the claims are returned unfiltered. `locate`
defaults to `false`.

Accepts up to 50,000 characters (longer input is truncated). Free for
API-key holders, capped at 1000 calls per ACCOUNT per day (resets at
00:00 UTC) regardless of input length — a focused call costs the same one
unit as an unfocused one. The cap is shared across all of the account's
keys.

from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
claims = client.extract(text="Coffee causes cancer and the earth is flat.")
# Add language="es" to return extracted claims in Spanish.
for c in claims.identified_claims:
    print(c)

post.description:
Resolve a multi-claim interrupt by selecting one or more of the offered
claims.

Each selected claim fans out into its own independent pipeline (like
``/verify/batch``), so the response is batch-shaped:
``{batch_id, items: [{task_id, claim_text}], partial?}``. Poll each
``task_id`` via ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}``.

Send the chosen claims in ``claims`` (``texts`` is accepted as an alias).
Every selected claim must match one that was offered in the prior
``needs_input`` response (server-validated against the recorded offer set);
arbitrary client-asserted text is rejected.

get.description:
Poll processing status for a submitted verification.

Four shapes keyed on ``status`` — ``processing``, ``needs_input``,
``completed``, ``failed`` — and only the fields belonging to the current
one are present (see the response schema). A field that does not belong
to the current shape is omitted rather than sent as null, so a client may
test for presence.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

# typed progress needs lenz-io >= 2.11.0
client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
status = client.get_status("tsk_abc123")

# "processing" | "needs_input" | "completed" | "failed"
if status.status == "processing":
    p = status.progress
    print(f"{p.step} — step {p.index} of {p.total}")
elif status.status == "completed":
    print(status.result.verdict, status.result.key_finding)

get.description:
Return the calling account's credit balance and what it can still buy.

**``credits`` is the balance.** One pool funds every billable capability,
at the weights in ``costs`` — today ``verify`` 10, ``assess`` 1, ``ask`` 1.
It has two buckets: the monthly allowance for the current ``plan``, which
resets at ``resets_at``, and non-expiring ``extra`` credits from grants and
top-ups, spent only once the allowance is gone. ``remaining`` is the sum,
and is what a call is actually checked against.

``credits.bonus`` is the deprecated old name of ``credits.extra``, the same
number, deprecated with the fields below and kept for existing callers. Read ``extra``.

``plan`` is the stable slug to branch on; ``plan_label`` is the same tier
as display copy ("Pro"). Two fields rather than one humanised
string, so a reworded label cannot break a client comparing tiers.
The Pro plan's ``plan`` is ``pro``; it read ``developer`` before
2026-09-15 (#664), while ``plan_label`` already read "Pro".

**The per-capability blocks are deprecated.** ``verify`` / ``ask`` /
``assess`` are **projections** of that one pool into each capability's own
unit — "how many of these could I still make" — not separate allowances.
Spending on one moves all of them, and they are floor divisions, so a
verify block ticks once per 10 credits spent anywhere.

They are deprecated, together with the per-block ``credits`` alias, and
kept for existing callers. Derive them instead::

    remaining = credits.remaining // costs[capability]
    total     = credits.total     // costs[capability]
    used      = total - remaining

Two capabilities at the same price emit identical blocks — ``ask`` and
``assess`` are both 1 credit — which is the clearest sign the shape
describes an allowance that no longer exists.

``bonus`` in each block is ``credits.extra`` in that capability's unit. The
older key ``credits`` is its deprecated alias, on the same date.

``costs`` is one entry per capability at its DEFAULT price. Prices that
depend on a request parameter live in ``cost_options``, nested capability
→ parameter → value — ``{"verify": {"depth": {"standard": 10, "low": 5}}}``.
Two maps rather than a flat one with a ``verify_low`` key, so a future
tuning parameter nests instead of adding an entry that reads like a fifth
capability. Every capability in ``cost_options`` also appears in ``costs``
at its default, so reading only ``costs`` is always correct.

``extract`` is free at the pool (``costs.extract`` is 0) and is bounded by
a per-account daily fair-use cap instead, reported separately here and
rejected with 429 rather than 402.

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
u = client.usage()
# One credit pool funds every call; `costs` is the price list.
print(u.credits.remaining, "credits left", u.costs)
# The same balance, projected into one capability's unit.
print(u.verify.remaining, "verify calls left")
print(u.assess.remaining, "assess calls left")
print(u.credits.extra, "of them extra credits (grants and top-ups, never expiring)")

get.description:
Retrieve the full verification report for a single claim.

Returns the verdict, citations, and (under ``audit``) the panel
reasoning, debate transcript, and assessments. Same shape as the
/verify webhook payload and the deprecated /library/{id} endpoint
this merger replaces.

Authorization model (optional Bearer):
- Anon callers see any listed public claim (``visibility='public'`` AND
  ``status`` in {pending, published}) PLUS any API ``unlisted`` claim
  (``visibility='public'``, ``status='hidden'``, ``source_channel='api'``):
  unlisted is readable by verification_id, just never surfaced in listings.
- Authed callers additionally see their own claims regardless of
  visibility or status.
- Private claims, and non-API hidden public claims (retracted / pre-screen),
  owned by someone else return 404.

Also accepts the **task_id** ``/verify`` returned, in place of a
verification_id. A completed run reads exactly as its verification_id
would. A run that has not completed answers **409** with ``status``
(``processing``, ``needs_input`` or ``failed``) and a ``hint``, plus the
failure fields when it failed; poll ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}`` for
progress. A task_id that is unknown, or not yours, answers 404 with a
``hint`` at that endpoint.

delete.description:
Delete an owned verification.

Removes the verification, its analysis, evidence and follow-up chat, and
the text of each request that submitted it from your credit history and
from our API-call log (on a batch, that item only). Not reached by a
deletion: copies in our caches, which expire within 24 hours, and our
backups, which age out within 60 days.

Deleting a warranted verification keeps its certificate and warranty; the
certificate stays at its `certificate_url`.

get.description:
Download the warranty certificate for a covered verification.

Resolved by (verification, ACCOUNT), not by verification alone: one cached
analysis can have several holders, each with their own certificate, their
own cap and their own link. Returning "the certificate for this
verification" would hand one customer another customer's document.

Byte-identical to ``/certificate/<certificate_id>.json``. A withdrawn
certificate is still served — it is the record of what was warranted, and
the withdrawal date is on it.

Served whether or not new certificates are currently being issued: an
issued certificate stands.

List public verifications semantically related to this one.

Returns the closest public-library claims by semantic similarity
(cosine distance, 0 = identical). Excludes the verification itself,
near-duplicates (distance < 0.2), and editorially-hidden claims. Empty
list when the verification has not been indexed yet (that happens
shortly after it completes) or when no claim is close enough.

Authorization model (optional Bearer) — identical to
``GET /verifications/{verification_id}``: anon callers reach listed public claims plus
API-origin unlisted ones; a valid key additionally unlocks the
caller's own claims. Results are always drawn from the public
library only, so keyless access exposes nothing new.
``limit`` is clamped to [1, 10].

x-codeSamples.source:
from lenz_io import Lenz

client = Lenz(api_key="lenz_...")
related = client.verifications.related("vid_abc123", limit=5)
for r in related.items:
    print(r.verification_id, r.claim, r.verdict)

get.description: Get ask history and remaining quota for a verification.

delete.description: Delete all ask messages for this user on a verification.

post.description:
Send a question and get an expert response.

The reply (``content`` field on the response) is plain text with a
small markdown subset baked in by the chat model:

- ``**bold**`` and ``*italic*``
- ``- `` or ``* `` bullet lists
- Blank-line paragraph breaks; single newlines inside a paragraph
  mean line break
- ``[label](url)`` links, only ever to one of the verification's
  sources: any other link is reduced to its label before the reply
  is returned

The model only produces these — no headings, no tables, no code
blocks. Pass the reply through any markdown library or display it
verbatim.

Documented at https://lenz.io/docs/quickstart#ask-reply-format.

422.description: The body names a field or a value the endpoint does not take.

example.detail: payload.escalate.verdicts: Unknown verdict label 'Misleading'; use one of: False, Mostly False, Mixed, Mostly True, True.

errors.msg: Unknown verdict label 'Misleading'; use one of: False, Mostly False, Mixed, Mostly True, True.

post.description:
Read a draft, quick-check every claim, deep-check the ones that look
wrong or uncertain, and hand back the issues with the fixes.

Returns 202 with a `review_id`; read the review at the `Location`
(`GET /reviews/{review_id}`), or receive `review.completed` /
`review.failed` at your webhook. A review takes two to four minutes.

It spends the credits the primitives spend: 1 per claim assessed, and 10
(5 at `depth: low`) per deep check it runs. At most
`min(claims, max_assessments) × 1 + max_verifications × depth cost`;
the review reports what it charged.

Send `escalate.max_citations: N` to also check the draft's first N
citations (markdown links, bare URLs, DOIs, `[n]` markers with a reference
list): for each, whether the source says what the draft attributes to it.
Off by default; 1 credit per checked citation, and a source that could not
be checked is not charged. `POST /citecheck` is the same check alone.
The rows are in `citations[]`, the ones that do not hold up in
`citation_issues[]`, and `outcome` reads `issues_found` for them.
`escalate.max_assessments: 0` runs no quick check (a review of the
citations alone).

Only claims traced directly back to the draft are checked: a claim found
nowhere in it is left out (as `/extract` does with `locate: true`). Each
claim row's `positions` says where the draft makes it, and
`more_claim_locations` gives `{claim, positions}` for each of
`more_claims`. Claim and citation positions share one shape, `{start, end,
text}`: `start` / `end` in Unicode code points of `text` as you sent it,
half-open, and `text` the passage (`null` on a citation, whose row carries
the statement). For a URL draft `start` / `end` are `null` and `text`
carries the passage.

A `text` that is one URL is read like `/extract` reads it and counts as
one `/extract` call: past the daily `/extract` limit it answers 429
`extract_daily_limit`. The other 429 is `review_in_flight` (three reviews
running on the account).

x-codeSamples.source:
curl -X POST https://lenz.io/api/v1/review \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer lenz_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Idempotency-Key: draft-42" \
  -d '{"text": "The EU AI Act took effect in March 2024. ...",
       "escalate": {"max_verifications": 5}}'
# 202 {"review_id": "a1b2c3d4", "status": "queued"}
# Location: /api/v1/reviews/a1b2c3d4

Check whether each cited source says what the draft attributes to it.

Send `text` (a draft with its links: markdown links, bare URLs, `doi:` and

send (or `max_citations` for a text), and a citation that could not be
checked is refunded. `credits.charged` on the check says what it cost.

The check as it stands. Poll no faster than `poll_after_seconds`; read

An entity (person, place, organization, concept) referenced in the
submitted claim.

``qid`` is the Wikidata Q identifier (e.g. ``Q42`` for Douglas Adams)
when Lenz resolved the entity against its internal catalog; ``null``
otherwise. Customers can join on ``qid`` to their own Wikidata-indexed
corpus, or hit the Wikidata API directly for richer metadata.

Single item in a list of verifications.

Used by both ``GET /library`` (public catalog) and
``GET /verifications`` (authed-owner listing). Slim shape — no
``url`` (customers reference claims by ``verification_id``), no
``visibility`` (API claims are private by default; the field had
zero information value on the listing surface).

suggested_rewrite.description: A suggested rewrite of `claim` that this verification's findings support, to use in place of the original sentence. It has not been verified itself: before using it, review it or run it through `/verify`. `null` for a true claim, when no correction is established, and on verifications that predate the field. On every verification, single or listed; not on `/assess` rows.

AssessClaimOut.description:
Per-claim entry inside an ``AssessOut.claims`` list.

A verdict row is the entire answer for that claim. ``verification_url``
is set when a full verification of the same claim exists and the caller
can read it; follow it for sources, reasoning and the deep score.

``rationale`` is the reasoning of a reviewer who agrees with the panel's
verdict; ``dissent``, when set, is the reasoning of the reviewer farthest
from it. Both are reviewers' notes, not checked sources; for sourced
evidence, call /verify.

Same field vocabulary as ``ClaimDetailOut`` (``claim``, ``verdict``,
``confidence``); /assess omits ``lenz_score``, which only a full
verification computes. ``language`` echoes the output language so a
batch caller can route per-claim text when items differ in language.

``suggested_rewrite`` is on every row: the claim with its wrong part
corrected when the request set ``suggest_rewrite`` and the check found the
claim False or Mostly False with high confidence; ``null`` when it was not
requested, the row is outside that, or there was no correction to write. It
is not itself verified: review it, or run it through /verify.

The three trailing keys are emitted on EVERY row (empty on a plain
verdict row) so the shape is one shape: ``error_code`` says why a
``verdict: Error`` row has no verdict (``no_claim`` | ``framing_failed`` |
``upstream_unavailable`` | ``timeout`` — an OPEN set: branch on the values
you know and fall through on the rest, because a new one can be added
without a major version. ``timeout`` means the call ran out of its time
budget on that item; it is free and worth resending, unlike
``framing_failed``, which is deterministic). A vague item is assessed on
its most likely reading, which ``claim`` carries; ``candidate_claims`` is
always ``[]`` and is kept only so released SDK models keep parsing.
``identified_claims`` lists the OTHER claims found in a list item that
were NOT assessed (the list form assesses one claim per item, the
primary). ``hint`` is one sentence on what to send next — set on every
Error row and on a verdict row whose item held more claims than the one
assessed; ``None`` on a plain verdict row. On an Error row ``claim``
echoes the item as submitted.
AssessClaimOut.title: AssessClaimOut

AssessOut.description:
Response body for ``POST /assess``.

``error_code`` is the machine-readable companion to ``error``: ``'no_claim'``
when the text holds no checkable claim (a vague input is assessed on its
most likely reading instead). ``candidate_claims`` is always ``[]`` and
is kept only so released SDK models keep parsing. Both are absent/empty
on the happy path.

more_claims.description: Claims found in a single `text` past the ones checked: one call checks at most 20, ranked most check-worthy first. Not checked and not charged; send them as `claims` (up to 20 a call) to check them. Always `[]` for the `claims` list form.
more_claims.title: More Claims

AssessOut.title: AssessOut

AssessIn.description:
Request body for ``POST /assess``.

Two forms. ``claim`` (or its alias ``text``) is ONE text: read once and
expanded, so every claim found in it becomes a row (up to 20, one credit
each; a text that makes more lists the rest in ``more_claims``). ``claims`` is a list
of up to 20 items: exactly one row per item, in order — the batch rung of
the extract → assess → verify ladder. Sending both is a 422.

claim.description: The claim to check. A statement in natural language; several claims in one string are split and handled separately.
claim.title: Claim

text.description: Accepted alias for `claim`. Send one or the other; `text` is used when it has content.
text.title: Text

claims.description: A list of up to 20 — one verdict row each, in order. Use this for the claims `/extract` returned; each item is one claim (≤2000 chars), not a document. Mutually exclusive with `claim`.
claims.title: Claims

suggest_rewrite.description: Also write `suggested_rewrite` on each row: the claim with its wrong part corrected, for a claim the check found False or Mostly False with high confidence. Off by default. It costs no extra credit and works in both forms, per row. The rewrite comes from the quick check's reasoning and is not itself verified: review it, or run it through `/verify`, before using it.
suggest_rewrite.title: Suggest Rewrite

claim.description: The claim, exactly as it appears in the claim list it belongs to.
claim.title: Claim

positions.description: Every place the text makes the claim, in text order, at most 10. `null` only when this claim could not be placed (on /extract every returned claim was placed).
positions.title: Positions

ExtractOut.description:
The claims found in the submitted text.

`claim` is the most check-worthy claim. `identified_claims` is the
complete ordered list when more than one claim was found (the top claim
included — iterate it on its own) and `[]` for a single claim.

`status` is `ready` when claims were found, `not_a_claim` when the text
contains no verifiable factual claim, and `no_match` when a `focus` was
given and no claim falls within it.

With `locate: true`, only claims traced back to the text are listed, and
`locations` gives the passages that make each one.

locations.description: Only with `locate: true`: where the text makes each returned claim, one entry per claim in the order of `identified_claims` (one entry for a single `claim`). `[]` when every claim was left out (`status` is then `not_a_claim`). `null` when `locate` was not set, when the extraction found no claims, or when the claims could not be located.
locations.title: Locations

ExtractOut.title: ExtractOut

start.description: Where the passage starts in `text` as you sent it, in Unicode code points (not UTF-16 units or bytes). Half-open with `end`. `null` when `text` was a URL: the page is not returned, so there is nothing to index, and `text` carries the passage instead.
start.title: Start

end.description: Where the passage ends, exclusive; `null` as for `start`.
end.title: End

text.description: The passage itself, as it appears in the text. `null` on a citation position, whose row already carries the statement.
text.title: Text

text.description: The document to extract claims from. Up to 50,000 characters; longer input is truncated. Or a single public web page URL (http or https, nothing else in the field): Lenz reads the page, or a YouTube video's transcript, and extracts the claims from its first 50,000 characters.
text.title: Text

language.description: ISO 639-1 code for the language of the emitted claims. Defaults to the input's language.
language.title: Language

focus.description: Optional. Narrows the result to the claims this describes, e.g. "market size, growth and competitors". At most 300 characters — a longer focus is rejected, never truncated. A focus can only select from the claims the extractor found: it cannot add a claim, reword one, reorder them, or change what counts as a claim. When nothing matches, `status` is `no_match` and `identified_claims` is empty; the unfocused list is never substituted.
focus.title: Focus

locate.description: Optional, default `false`. When `true`, only claims that could be traced directly back to your text are returned, and `locations` says where in the text each one is made. A claim found nowhere in the text, or found with a different figure, is left out; so is a list that ends up empty, which answers `not_a_claim`. Adds a few seconds, never more than 20. If the claims cannot be located, `locations` is `null` and the list is returned unfiltered.
locate.title: Locate

claims.description: The claims to verify, as strings: the `text` of each entry in the status response's `claims`, copied verbatim.
claims.title: Claims

texts.description: Accepted alias for `claims`. Send one or the other; `texts` is used when it has content.
texts.title: Texts

AssessmentOut.description:
An adjudicator's individual assessment. Nested under ``audit``.

Current verifications carry three independent reviewers (``Reviewer A``
to ``Reviewer C``), each assigned a model from a different vendor (after a
provider failure a reviewer can run on another vendor's model), and two
more (``Reviewer D``, ``Reviewer E``) when those three disagree, all
running the same checks over the evidence; ``warnings`` carries the source
issues, evidence gaps and precision issues that reviewer found, in one
list. ``panelist_name`` is a display value, not a stable key.
Verifications from before the change carry the specialist panelists
instead, one flag category each: logical fallacies (Logic Examiner),
precision issues (Precision Analyst), weakest sources (Source Auditor)
and, before 2026-06, missing context (Context Analyst).
AssessmentOut.title: AssessmentOut

AuditOut.description:
Audit / explainability block — for callers that need to show their work.

``panel_agreement`` is derived from the panel: ``unanimous`` (all agree),
``majority`` (score spread <= 2), or ``split`` — over every reviewer that
voted, so a panel that called in Reviewers D and E is counted whole.
AuditOut.title: AuditOut

CandidateClaimOut.description:
A single candidate claim surfaced when the framing detects multiple
distinct claims in the submitted text. The caller picks one via
``POST /verify/{task_id}/select``.
CandidateClaimOut.title: CandidateClaimOut

ClaimDetailOut.description:
Full verification report.

Slim top-level (verdict + confidence + lenz_score + sources). Audit
detail (panel reasoning, debate, individual panelist assessments)
lives under ``audit``.

Same field vocabulary as ``VerificationListItemOut`` (list view) and
``AssessClaimOut`` (fast verdict). A consumer that branches on
``verdict`` or ``confidence`` reads the same field name regardless
of which endpoint produced the payload.

suggested_rewrite.description: A suggested rewrite of `claim` that this verification's findings support, to use in place of the original sentence. It has not been verified itself: before using it, review it or run it through `/verify`. `null` for a true claim, when no correction is established, and on verifications that predate the field. On every verification, single or listed; not on `/assess` rows.
suggested_rewrite.title: Suggested Rewrite

ClaimDetailOut.title: ClaimDetailOut

CoverageOut.description:
Whether this verdict carries a warranty, and if not, why not.

Present only when covered verification is enabled. It describes the pair
(this account, this analysis), not the analysis alone: two accounts can
hold two certificates over one cached verdict, so the block one customer
sees is never the block another sees.

``reasons`` is empty exactly when ``status`` is not ``uncovered``. The
vocabulary is closed and deliberately smaller than the internal gate's:
``plan`` and ``depth`` are actionable, ``account`` means the account
turned certificates off (Pro and Scale), ``verdict`` is a product rule
callers design around, ``quality`` covers everything a caller can neither
act on nor define, and ``withdrawn`` / ``issue_failed`` are statements
about Lenz rather than about the caller's claim.
CoverageOut.title: CoverageOut

DebateSideOut.description: One side of the debate (pro or con). Nested under ``audit``.
DebateSideOut.title: DebateSideOut

ProgressOut.description:
Where a running verification has got to. Advisory — never results.

``step`` is a closed set, so it is safe to switch on. ``index`` is the
1-based stage position (0 while ``starting``) out of ``total``; read
``total`` off the response rather than hard-coding it, since stages may
be added.

``index`` is stage POSITION, not elapsed work: the stages are uneven, so
a client rendering it as a bar will see it sit on ``research`` for roughly
half the run. ``elapsed_seconds`` is a measurement of how long the run has
been going, never an estimate of what is left.
ProgressOut.title: ProgressOut

SourceOut.description:
A research source used to evaluate a claim.

``date`` is the source article's publication date (a source-level
attribute, not a Lenz API event time — so it's not renamed to
``published_at``).

snippet.description: The sentence(s) quoted from the source page, verbatim and in the page's own language, with ` … ` between separate passages. A few sources carry no verified quote — for those it is the surrounding passage instead, which may run longer and contain line breaks.
snippet.title: Snippet

SourceOut.title: SourceOut

StatusOut.description:
Body of ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}``.

Four shapes keyed on ``status``, and only the fields belonging to the
current one are present — ``processing`` carries ``progress``,
``needs_input`` carries ``reason`` plus ``claims``, ``completed``
carries ``result``,
and ``failed`` carries the error block. Branch on ``status`` and read
the fields for that branch; absent is meaningful, so do not treat a
missing key as an empty one.

``task_id`` is echoed on every shape, so a caller polling several
verifications in one loop can tell the replies apart without threading
the id through their own call site.
StatusOut.title: StatusOut

MeUsageCreditsOut.description:
The account's credit balance — the one pool every capability spends.

Two buckets: the monthly allowance for the current plan (resets at
``resets_at``) and non-expiring ``extra`` credits from grants and top-ups,
which are spent only once the allowance is gone. ``remaining`` is the sum
and is what a call is checked against.

``bonus`` is a DEPRECATED alias of ``extra`` (the balance's name until
2026-09-15), deprecated with the other deprecated fields on this endpoint and kept
for existing callers. It was renamed because the balance holds top-ups you paid for as
well as grants.
MeUsageCreditsOut.title: MeUsageCreditsOut

MeUsageExtractOut.title: MeUsageExtractOut

MeUsageOut.description:
The calling account's credit balance, and what it can still buy.

``credits`` is the balance and ``costs`` is the price list. Those two,
plus ``cost_options``, are the whole contract for a new integration.

The ``verify`` / ``ask`` / ``assess`` blocks are DEPRECATED projections of
that same pool into each capability's unit, kept for clients
already reading them.

``extract`` is free at the pool (``costs.extract`` is 0) and carries a
per-account daily fair-use cap instead; it rejects with 429, not 402.

The Pro plan's ``plan`` is ``pro`` since 2026-09-15; it was ``developer``
before (#664). ``plan_label`` reads "Pro" either way.
MeUsageOut.title: MeUsageOut

MeUsageQuotaOut.description:
DEPRECATED. One capability's share of the pool, projected into its unit.

**Deprecated**, with the per-block ``credits`` alias below, and kept for
existing callers. Read
``MeUsageOut.credits`` and ``MeUsageOut.costs`` instead and do the
division — it is one line, and it is the same one this block does::

    remaining = credits.remaining // costs[capability]
    total     = credits.total     // costs[capability]
    used      = total - remaining

These are **projections, not allowances**. Every billable capability draws
on the single balance in ``MeUsageOut.credits``, at the weight in
``MeUsageOut.costs``; this block answers "how many ``/verify`` calls could
I still make if I spent everything on them". Spending on any capability
moves every block, and the division floors — a ``verify`` block whose
weight is 10 ticks once per 10 credits spent anywhere.

They predate the pool, when each really was its own allowance, and that is
the reason to retire them: two capabilities at the same price emit
byte-identical objects (``ask`` and ``assess`` are both 1 credit today),
so the shape suggests a per-capability allowance that no longer exists.

``bonus`` is ``MeUsageOut.credits.extra``, the non-expiring balance, in
this capability's unit.
``quota_used`` is derived as ``quota_total - quota_remaining``, so
``used + remaining == total`` always holds.

``credits`` is a DEPRECATED alias of ``bonus``, kept for compatibility
with existing callers. It never meant the pool — before the pool existed it
meant this capability's one-off top-up balance, which is exactly what
``bonus`` now reports.
MeUsageQuotaOut.title: MeUsageQuotaOut

VerificationNotFoundOut.title: VerificationNotFoundOut

VerificationNotReadyOut.description:
409 from ``GET /verifications/{id}`` for a task_id with no result yet.

The endpoint accepts the task_id ``/verify`` returned, and a completed run
reads exactly as its verification_id would. A run that has not completed
has no verification to return, so it answers 409. ``status`` says why:
still ``processing``, waiting on
``needs_input``, or ``failed``. Poll ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}`` for
progress, the options a ``needs_input`` run offers, or the full failure.

The failure fields are present on ``failed`` only.
VerificationNotReadyOut.title: VerificationNotReadyOut

VerificationPurgedOut.description:

Answered by ``GET /verifications/{id}``, ``GET /verify/status/{task_id}``
for a completed task, ``/related`` and ``/ask``, and only to a caller who
could read the verification: anyone else gets the usual 404. The
certificate of a covered verification stays available.

so values run 1 through 4 (initial + 3 retries).
